title: How To Handle Students Who Will Ruin Your Day If You Hold Them Accountable day-if-you-hold-them-accountable/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Note: the batch's supplied date (May 22, 2023) is a later revision/edit date; the article's URL and published_time meta tag both confirm the true original publish date of June 28, 2014, which is used here. Linsin addresses teachers who have become effectively held hostage by a difficult student whose past reactions to consequences—tantrums, arguing, scene-making—have taught the teacher to look the other way. He argues this appeasement pattern only deepens the problem, since avoiding accountability signals that the student is exempt from the rules that govern everyone else. His prescribed solution is to hold the student accountable anyway, delivering the consequence calmly and disengaging from however they react, whether that's arguing, crying, or disruption. He acknowledges the student's reaction may not improve immediately or even get worse before it gets better, but insists that consistent, unemotional follow-through eventually earns the student's trust. The piece closes with a note clarifying this is meant for teachers already in a bad pattern, and that starting with consistent accountability from day one is the better long-term solution.
points: Repeatedly avoiding consequences for a volatile student due to past bad reactions creates a demoralizing power imbalance.
The fix is to hold the student accountable anyway, delivering the consequence calmly and disengaging regardless of the reaction.
The student's reaction to accountability (arguing, tantrums, disruption) is not the teacher's concern to manage in the moment.
Consistent follow-through, even when the initial reaction stays bad or worsens, gradually earns the student's trust over time.
The author notes this is a recovery strategy for teachers already stuck in appeasement, while starting with consistent accountability from day one remains the better path.
quotes: You’ll have to give up your leverage and authority and treat them differently than everyone else.
So now this one student, all of eight years old—or four or thirteen—has you over a barrel and the best you can hope for is to ignore them and cross your fingers that they don’t become too disruptive.
How they handle it isn’t your concern. If they argue, don’t respond. If they throw themselves on the floor, leave them be.
And when they break another rule? Do it again. Follow your plan. Their reaction may be as bad as the first time—perhaps worse—but before long, if you stick with it, it will get better.

You see, when you offer your students real-world truth and acceptance, when you stop tiptoeing around them and instead show your faith in them and who they can become by never letting misbehavior go . . .
